The total quality score was calculated, with a score of 20 indicating strong quality, 10-15 indicating moderate quality, and less than 10 indicating weak quality. Study Characteristics and Details: The study by Manickam (2016) was a single-arm open-field trial aimed at determining the efficacy of preventing a 5-year cumulative 5% relapse rate, as well as assessing acceptability, safety, and compliance. Newly detected and untreated leprosy patients were enrolled from six centers in India and two centers in China between October 2003 and June 2008. Patients received U-MDT (supervised pulse doses of rifampicin, clofazimine, and dapsone every 4 weeks, along with daily unsupervised doses of clofazimine and dapsone). The follow-up period lasted 5 years, with the final follow-up completed in January 2014. A total of 3,437 patients were screened, and 3,389 were enrolled. Outcomes Assessed: Special events included new lesions, relapses, reactions, disabilities, neuritis, and other events. Treatment was deemed acceptable across all centers, with no complaints about clofazimine pigmentation. The dropout rate at the end of the study was reported, with an initial sample size of 3,389 and a final sample size of 2,789. Statistical Analysis: Statistical methods included t-tests for continuous variables, chi-square tests for dichotomous variables, Kaplan-Meier methods for the frequency of first reactions, Poisson regression for recurrent reactions, and logistic regression to evaluate associations. Additional Studies: The study by Penna (2012) was an open randomized controlled trial (RCT) aimed at evaluating the association between treatment duration and the frequency of reactions in MB patients. The study by Penna (2014) was an open-label RCT assessing the association between treatment duration and the trend in bacterial index (BI) over time among patients receiving U-MDT. The study by Penna (2017) was an RCT focusing on a subgroup of patients with MB leprosy to assess outcomes. Quality Ratings: Studies were rated as Good, Fair, or Poor based on criteria such as randomization, blinding, follow-up duration, and reporting of outcomes. For randomized controlled trials, the quality of random allocation concealment, group comparability at baseline, and blinding of healthcare providers and outcome assessors were evaluated. Follow-up time, dropout details, and the use of validated outcome measures were also considered.
